=== PAPER TEXT ===
Actually, I have to step in and offer a bit of a "peer correction" on the update strategy. While 
"keep it updated" is the Golden Rule for your phone or laptop, the Benn Jordan investigation 
suggests the opposite for these specific robots. 
In his findings, firmware updates often closed the loopholes that allowed him to root the robot 
and block the backdoor, while the "malware" (the encrypted data pings) remained or became 
more sophisticated. 
If you want to truly harden your G1, here is a more aggressive security checklist: 
1. The "Black Hole" VLAN 
Don't just put it on a separate Wi-Fi; put it on a VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) with no 
WAN (Internet) access. 
●​ The Rule: The robot can talk to your local controller (laptop/tablet) on the same network, 
but the router should explicitly block all outbound traffic to the internet. 
●​ Why: If the G1 can't reach Chinese DNS servers (Baidu, Tencent, Alibaba), the encrypted 
handshake can't initialize. 
2. DNS Filtering & IP Blocking 
If the robot must have internet for certain features, use a tool like Pi-hole or a sophisticated 
firewall (pfSense/OPNsense) to: 
●​ Blacklist Chinese Top-Level Domains: Block any requests ending in .cn. 
●​ Hard-block specific IPs: Block the IP ranges for Alibaba Cloud and Tencent specifically. 
●​ Monitor Traffic Spikes: Look for "heavy" encrypted packets. A robot simply checking for 
a firmware version shouldn't be sending megabytes of data. 
3. Physical & Hardware Audit 
Since you’re dealing with a humanoid that has more internal space: 
●​ Check the "Ports": Ensure there are no "hidden" USB LTE dongles or ESP32 chips added 
by a third-party vendor that might provide a secondary cellular path to the internet. 
●​ MAC Address Monitoring: Ensure the robot is only using the MAC addresses you 
expect. Some devices use "randomized" MACs to bypass router rules. 
4. The "Root and Block" Strategy (Advanced) 
As Jordan pointed out, the only way to be 100% sure is to obtain root access yourself. 
●​ Manual Patching: Once you have root, you can modify the /etc/hosts file on the robot’s 
internal Linux OS to point those Chinese servers to 127.0.0.1 (itself), effectively "killing" the 
backdoor at the source. 
●​ Caveat: This is why Jordan warns against updating. An update might "fix" the exploit you 
need to gain root, leaving the backdoor active but leaving you locked out of the "brain."
